As someone who drives this car regularly, I’d like to clarify a few things that may have been unclear:

Customizable Glove Box Operation
The glove box can be customized for easy access. In my car, for instance, a long press on the volume button opens the glove box.

Dashcam Functionality via USB
The USB port located inside the glove box is used for dashcam recordings. It captures video from multiple external cameras—recording in all directions while the car is driving or parked. The interior camera is excluded from this recording setup.

Interior Camera Usage
The interior camera is not used for recording the driver passively. Instead, it tracks eye and head movement, especially when using Autopilot or Full Self-Driving features, to ensure driver attentiveness. It can also be used for video calls, such as Zoom meetings, when the vehicle is stationary.

"Fart Mode" Fun Feature
Beyond using the turn signal to activate the "fart" sound, you can also tap on a seat icon on the screen. The sound will play from the speaker closest to the selected seat, creating the illusion that the person sitting there is responsible for the sound.

Driving Behavior Customization
You can adjust the car’s driving behavior to mimic that of a traditional gasoline vehicle. For example, enabling “Creep” mode allows the car to decelerate more gradually, similar to how a conventional automatic car behaves.

Here is a list of the specific "safety" and "security" problems experts and politicians are currently debating:

1. The "Spy Car" Problem (Data Privacy)
Security experts, including former CSIS (Canadian Security Intelligence Service) officers, have called these vehicles "rolling spy vans" for a few reasons:

Constant Surveillance: These cars have multiple cameras, high-definition microphones, and GPS trackers. The concern is that they can record everything happening inside and outside the vehicle and send that data back to servers in China.

Legal Cooperation: Under Chinese law, companies like BYD or Xiaomi are required to cooperate with the Chinese government if asked for data, which could include mapping sensitive Canadian infrastructure or tracking specific people.

2. Remote Control Risk (Cybersecurity)
The biggest fear is that these cars are essentially computers on wheels that can be updated wirelessly.

"Kill Switch": Theoretically, if there were a conflict or diplomatic tension, a software update could be used to remotely disable the car or even take control of the steering and brakes while the car is driving.

Infrastructure Attacks: Because these cars plug into our electrical grid to charge, experts worry they could be used as a "portal" to launch cyberattacks against Canada's energy or communication networks.

3. Fire & Hardware Safety (The "Self-Burn" Issue)
There have been many viral videos of Chinese EVs catching fire, which has sparked a huge debate in China and now in Canada.

Thermal Runaway: Some Chinese batteries have been reported to engulf a car in flames in as little as 10 to 60 seconds, which doesn't leave much time for a family to escape.

Corner Cutting: To keep prices so low, some companies have been accused of skipping safety safeguards or using "ternary" batteries that are powerful but less stable than the ones used by companies like Hyundai.

4. "Ghost" Companies (Support Issues)
The Chinese EV market is overcrowded. Analysts predict that dozens of these brands will go bankrupt or shut down by the end of 2026.

If you buy a car from a company that disappears, you won't be able to get software updates, parts for repairs, or use your warranty. This makes the car "unsafe" to drive in the long run because it can't be maintained.
